newTreatments.name: Antiretroviral Therapy (TLD - Tenofovir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir)
newTreatments.summary: The standard first-line single-pill HIV regimen in South Africa, combining two NRTIs (tenofovir, lamivudine) with the integrase inhibitor dolutegravir. Taken once daily, it suppresses the virus to undetectable levels so it can't be transmitted (U=U) and keeps the immune system healthy.

newTreatments.name: Dolutegravir (Integrase Inhibitor)
newTreatments.summary: A potent, well-tolerated HIV integrase inhibitor that blocks the virus from inserting its genes into your cells. It's the backbone of modern antiretroviral therapy, has a high barrier to resistance, and is the preferred third agent in first-line treatment.

newTreatments.name: PrEP (Tenofovir/Emtricitabine)
newTreatments.summary: Pre-exposure prophylaxis: a daily pill taken by HIV-negative people at risk to prevent infection. Highly effective when taken consistently, it's a cornerstone of HIV prevention alongside condoms and testing.

newTreatments.name: Co-trimoxazole (Prophylactic Antibiotic)
newTreatments.summary: A combination antibiotic (sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim) given to people with HIV and low immunity to prevent opportunistic infections like PCP pneumonia. Also used to treat a range of bacterial infections.

newTreatments.name: Anti-TB Combination Therapy (Rifampicin/Isoniazid/Pyrazinamide/Ethambutol)
newTreatments.summary: The standard curative regimen for drug-sensitive tuberculosis: four antibiotics taken together for an intensive phase, then two for continuation. Completing the full course (usually 6 months) is essential to cure TB and prevent drug-resistant strains.

newTreatments.name: TB Preventive Therapy (Isoniazid)
newTreatments.summary: Isoniazid taken on its own (or with rifapentine) to stop latent TB infection from becoming active disease. Especially important for people living with HIV and close contacts of TB patients.

newTreatments.name: Bedaquiline (Anti-TB, Drug-Resistant)
newTreatments.summary: A newer oral medication central to treating multidrug-resistant TB. It blocks the energy-producing machinery of the TB bacterium and has transformed DR-TB into a largely curable, injection-free, oral treatment.

newTreatments.name: ACE Inhibitors (e.g. Enalapril, Lisinopril)
newTreatments.summary: Blood-pressure medications that relax blood vessels by blocking the angiotensin-converting enzyme. They protect the heart and kidneys and are first-line for hypertension, heart failure, and kidney disease, especially with diabetes.

newTreatments.name: ARBs (e.g. Losartan, Telmisartan)
newTreatments.summary: Angiotensin receptor blockers lower blood pressure and protect the kidneys, similar to ACE inhibitors but without the common dry cough. Used for hypertension, heart failure, and to slow chronic kidney disease.

newTreatments.name: Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g. Amlodipine)
newTreatments.summary: Blood-pressure medications that relax and widen arteries by blocking calcium entry into vessel walls. Amlodipine is a widely used, effective first-line option, particularly suited to many people of African ancestry.

newTreatments.name: Thiazide Diuretics (e.g. Hydrochlorothiazide)
newTreatments.summary: Water pills that help the kidneys remove excess salt and fluid, lowering blood pressure. They're an inexpensive, effective first-line antihypertensive often combined with other classes.

newTreatments.name: Loop Diuretics (e.g. Furosemide)
newTreatments.summary: Powerful water pills that clear fluid overload, easing breathlessness and swelling in heart failure and advanced kidney disease. They act quickly on the kidneys to remove excess salt and water.

newTreatments.name: Beta-Blockers (e.g. Bisoprolol, Carvedilol)
newTreatments.summary: Medications that slow the heart and reduce its workload. They're a core part of heart-failure therapy that improves survival, and are also used for high blood pressure and certain abnormal heart rhythms.

newTreatments.name: Inhaled Corticosteroid (Controller Inhaler)
newTreatments.summary: The cornerstone preventer inhaler for asthma, taken daily to calm airway inflammation and prevent attacks. Used consistently it dramatically reduces symptoms, flare-ups, and the need for reliever inhalers.

newTreatments.name: Reliever Inhaler (Short-Acting Beta-Agonist, e.g. Salbutamol)
newTreatments.summary: A quick-acting rescue inhaler that opens tight airways within minutes during an asthma or COPD flare. It relieves wheezing and breathlessness but is not a substitute for a daily controller inhaler.

newTreatments.name: Combination Inhaler (Steroid + Long-Acting Bronchodilator)
newTreatments.summary: A single inhaler pairing an inhaled steroid with a long-acting bronchodilator for sustained control of asthma and COPD. It both reduces inflammation and keeps airways open over many hours.

newTreatments.name: Long-Acting Bronchodilator Inhaler (LABA/LAMA)
newTreatments.summary: Maintenance inhalers for COPD that keep airways relaxed and open for 12-24 hours, easing breathlessness and reducing flare-ups. Often combined as a dual bronchodilator for moderate to severe disease.

newTreatments.name: Antiseizure Medication (e.g. Carbamazepine, Valproate, Levetiracetam)
newTreatments.summary: Daily medications that stabilise electrical activity in the brain to prevent seizures. Most people with epilepsy achieve good seizure control on a single well-chosen drug, allowing a normal, safe daily life.

newTreatments.name: Hydroxyurea (for Sickle Cell)
newTreatments.summary: A foundational sickle cell medication that boosts protective fetal haemoglobin, reducing painful crises, acute chest episodes, and the need for transfusions. Taken daily, it can substantially improve quality and length of life.

newTreatments.name: Penicillin Prophylaxis (Sickle Cell)
newTreatments.summary: Daily preventive penicillin given to young children with sickle cell disease to guard against life-threatening pneumococcal infections, to which they are especially vulnerable. A simple, life-saving measure paired with vaccination.

newTreatments.name: Folic Acid
newTreatments.summary: A B-vitamin supplement that supports the rapid production of red blood cells. It's routinely given in sickle cell disease and other chronic anaemias, and before/during pregnancy to prevent birth defects.

newTreatments.name: Tenofovir (Hepatitis B Antiviral)
newTreatments.summary: A once-daily antiviral that powerfully suppresses the hepatitis B virus, halting liver damage and lowering the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Treatment is usually long-term and well tolerated.

newTreatments.name: Entecavir (Hepatitis B Antiviral)
newTreatments.summary: A potent oral antiviral for chronic hepatitis B that keeps the virus suppressed with a high barrier to resistance. Taken daily, it protects the liver from ongoing inflammation and scarring.

newTreatments.name: Hepatitis B Vaccine
newTreatments.summary: A safe, highly effective vaccine that prevents hepatitis B infection and the liver disease and cancer it can cause. Given as a routine infant series and to at-risk adults.

newTreatments.name: Praziquantel (for Schistosomiasis)
newTreatments.summary: The curative single-course treatment for schistosomiasis (bilharzia), a parasitic infection from contaminated freshwater. It clears the worms quickly and is also used in community deworming campaigns.

newTreatments.name: Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (Antimalarial)
newTreatments.summary: The fast, curative first-line treatment for uncomplicated malaria, pairing artemisinin with a partner drug to wipe out the parasite and prevent resistance. Prompt treatment is critical to avoid severe, life-threatening disease.

newTreatments.name: Malaria Prophylaxis (Preventive Antimalarials)
newTreatments.summary: Preventive antimalarial tablets taken by travellers and some residents in high-risk areas to stop infection before it starts. Used alongside bed nets and insect repellent for layered protection.

newTreatments.name: Methotrexate (DMARD)
newTreatments.summary: The anchor disease-modifying drug for rheumatoid arthritis, taken weekly to calm the overactive immune system and prevent joint destruction. Starting it early changes the course of the disease and preserves function.

newTreatments.name: Sulfasalazine (DMARD)
newTreatments.summary: A disease-modifying antirheumatic drug used alone or with methotrexate to reduce joint inflammation and slow damage in rheumatoid arthritis. An affordable, well-established option.

newTreatments.name: Biologic DMARDs (e.g. TNF Inhibitors)
newTreatments.summary: Injectable targeted therapies that block specific immune signals driving rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases. Used when standard DMARDs aren't enough, they can bring inflammation under tight control.

newTreatments.name: Hydroxychloroquine (for Lupus & RA)
newTreatments.summary: A foundational antimalarial-derived drug used long-term in lupus and rheumatoid arthritis to reduce flares, protect organs, and improve survival. It's gentle on the immune system and a cornerstone of lupus care.

newTreatments.name: Oral Corticosteroids (e.g. Prednisone)
newTreatments.summary: Powerful anti-inflammatory tablets used in short bursts or low doses to control flares of autoimmune disease, asthma, and other inflammatory conditions. Effective and fast-acting, they're used carefully to limit side effects.

newTreatments.name: Immunosuppressants (e.g. Azathioprine, Mycophenolate)
newTreatments.summary: Medications that dampen an overactive immune system to protect organs in lupus and other autoimmune diseases, particularly when the kidneys or other organs are involved. Used to induce and maintain remission.

newTreatments.name: Allopurinol (Urate-Lowering Therapy)
newTreatments.summary: The mainstay long-term medication for gout, taken daily to lower uric acid levels and dissolve the crystals that cause attacks. Consistent use prevents future flares and joint damage.

newTreatments.name: Colchicine (Anti-Inflammatory for Gout)
newTreatments.summary: An anti-inflammatory used to settle acute gout flares and to prevent them when starting urate-lowering therapy. It targets the specific inflammation triggered by urate crystals.

newTreatments.name: NSAIDs (Anti-Inflammatory Painkillers, e.g. Ibuprofen)
newTreatments.summary: Common anti-inflammatory painkillers used for gout flares, osteoarthritis, and other painful inflammatory conditions. They relieve pain and swelling but are used cautiously in people with kidney, heart, or stomach concerns.

newTreatments.name: Oral Iron Supplements (e.g. Ferrous Sulfate)
newTreatments.summary: Iron tablets that replenish the body's stores to correct iron-deficiency anaemia, restoring energy and healthy red blood cells. Treating the underlying cause of the iron loss is just as important as the supplement.

newTreatments.name: Intravenous Iron
newTreatments.summary: Iron given directly into a vein to rapidly correct iron-deficiency anaemia when oral iron isn't tolerated, isn't working, or stores need replenishing quickly. Often used in kidney disease and heavy menstrual blood loss.

newTreatments.name: Antipsychotic Medication (e.g. Risperidone, Olanzapine)
newTreatments.summary: The mainstay treatment for schizophrenia, helping to reduce hallucinations, delusions, and disordered thinking. Taken consistently alongside psychosocial support, they help people stay well and engaged in daily life.

newTreatments.name: Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotic
newTreatments.summary: An antipsychotic given as an injection every few weeks instead of daily pills, helping maintain steady treatment for schizophrenia. It eases the burden of remembering daily doses and reduces relapse.

newTreatments.name: Statins (Cholesterol-Lowering, e.g. Atorvastatin)
newTreatments.summary: Daily medications that lower cholesterol and stabilise artery plaque, cutting the risk of heart attack and stroke. They're a key part of secondary prevention after a stroke or heart disease.

newTreatments.name: Antiplatelet Therapy (e.g. Aspirin, Clopidogrel)
newTreatments.summary: Medications that make blood platelets less sticky to prevent clots, central to stopping a second stroke or heart attack. Low-dose aspirin or clopidogrel is a cornerstone of secondary prevention.

newTreatments.name: Anticoagulants (Blood Thinners, e.g. Warfarin, DOACs)
newTreatments.summary: Blood thinners that prevent dangerous clots, used to reduce stroke risk in conditions like atrial fibrillation and to treat clots. They require attention to dosing and, for some, regular monitoring.

newTreatments.name: Clot-Busting Therapy (Thrombolysis)
newTreatments.summary: An emergency treatment for acute ischaemic stroke that dissolves the blocking clot if given within a few hours of symptoms. Fast treatment can dramatically reduce long-term disability.

newTreatments.name: Naltrexone (for Alcohol Use Disorder)
newTreatments.summary: A medication that reduces alcohol cravings and the pleasurable 'reward' from drinking, supporting people in cutting down or staying abstinent. Used alongside counselling and support groups.

newTreatments.name: Acamprosate (for Alcohol Use Disorder)
newTreatments.summary: A relapse-prevention medication that helps stabilise brain chemistry disrupted by long-term drinking, easing the urge to drink during recovery. Best combined with psychosocial support.

newTreatments.name: Disulfiram (for Alcohol Use Disorder)
newTreatments.summary: A medication that causes an unpleasant reaction if alcohol is consumed, acting as a deterrent to support abstinence. Used in motivated people as part of a structured recovery plan.

newTreatments.name: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
newTreatments.summary: An essential B-vitamin given to people with alcohol use disorder to prevent serious brain damage (Wernicke's encephalopathy) caused by deficiency. A simple, protective supplement during recovery.

newTreatments.name: HPV Vaccine
newTreatments.summary: A vaccine that protects against the human papillomavirus strains that cause most cervical cancer. Given to adolescents before exposure, it is one of the most effective tools for preventing cervical cancer.

newTreatments.name: Cervical Screening (Pap Smear / HPV Test)
newTreatments.summary: A simple screening test that detects precancerous changes or HPV on the cervix before cancer develops, allowing early treatment. Regular screening is one of the most powerful ways to prevent cervical cancer deaths.

newTreatments.name: Chemotherapy
newTreatments.summary: Anti-cancer drugs that kill or slow rapidly dividing cancer cells, used to treat cervical and other cancers, sometimes alongside radiation or surgery. Treatment plans are tailored to the cancer type and stage.

newTreatments.name: Radiation Therapy
newTreatments.summary: Targeted high-energy radiation that destroys cancer cells, a key treatment for cervical cancer often combined with chemotherapy. It can be curative or used to relieve symptoms in advanced disease.

newTreatments.name: Dialysis (Haemodialysis / Peritoneal)
newTreatments.summary: A life-sustaining treatment for advanced kidney failure that filters waste and excess fluid from the blood when the kidneys can no longer do so. It is done regularly at a centre or at home while awaiting transplant.

newTreatments.name: Kidney Transplant
newTreatments.summary: Surgical replacement of failed kidneys with a healthy donor kidney, offering the best quality and length of life for many people with end-stage kidney disease. It requires lifelong anti-rejection medication.

newTreatments.name: SGLT2 Inhibitors (Kidney & Heart Protective)
newTreatments.summary: Once-daily tablets originally for diabetes that are now proven to slow chronic kidney disease and improve heart-failure outcomes, even without diabetes. They protect the kidneys and heart beyond their glucose-lowering effect.

newTreatments.name: Erythropoietin (Anaemia of Kidney Disease)
newTreatments.summary: An injectable hormone that stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells, treating the anaemia that often comes with advanced kidney disease. It restores energy and reduces the need for transfusions.

newTreatments.name: Physiotherapy
newTreatments.summary: Hands-on and exercise-based rehabilitation to restore movement, strength, and function after stroke, surgery, or injury, and to manage arthritis and chronic pain. A physiotherapist tailors a programme to your goals.

newTreatments.name: Stroke Rehabilitation
newTreatments.summary: A coordinated programme of physical, occupational, and speech therapy that helps people regain independence and skills after a stroke. Starting early and continuing consistently leads to the best recovery.

newTreatments.name: Occupational Therapy
newTreatments.summary: Therapy that helps people regain or adapt the everyday skills needed for daily living and work, whether after a stroke, with arthritis, or with a developmental condition. Focuses on practical independence and meaningful activity.

newTreatments.name: Speech and Language Therapy
newTreatments.summary: Therapy to rebuild communication and safe swallowing after a stroke or brain injury, and to support children with developmental and language difficulties. A speech therapist tailors exercises to each person's needs.

newTreatments.name: Pulmonary Rehabilitation
newTreatments.summary: A structured programme of supervised exercise, breathing techniques, and education for people with COPD and other lung diseases. It improves breathlessness, stamina, and confidence in daily activities.

newTreatments.name: Smoking Cessation Support
newTreatments.summary: Counselling and structured support to help people quit smoking, the single most important step in slowing COPD and reducing heart and cancer risk. Often combined with nicotine replacement or medication.

newTreatments.name: Nicotine Replacement Therapy
newTreatments.summary: Patches, gum, or lozenges that supply controlled nicotine to ease cravings and withdrawal while quitting smoking. They roughly double the chance of quitting successfully when paired with support.

newTreatments.name: Peer Support Groups (e.g. 12-Step / SMART Recovery)
newTreatments.summary: Facilitated peer groups where people facing the same condition share experience, accountability, and encouragement. Particularly valuable in alcohol and substance recovery, and for chronic illness coping.

newTreatments.name: Joint Replacement Surgery
newTreatments.summary: Surgical replacement of a severely damaged hip or knee joint with an artificial one, used for advanced osteoarthritis when other treatments no longer control pain. It can dramatically restore mobility and quality of life.

newTreatments.name: Weight Management
newTreatments.summary: Achieving and maintaining a healthier weight through diet and activity, which reduces load on arthritic joints, lowers blood pressure, and improves outcomes across many chronic conditions. First-line and often highly effective.

newTreatments.name: DASH / Low-Salt Diet
newTreatments.summary: An eating pattern rich in fruit, vegetables, and wholegrains and low in salt, proven to lower blood pressure. A central lifestyle measure for hypertension that also benefits the heart and kidneys.

newTreatments.name: Blood Transfusion
newTreatments.summary: Giving donor red blood cells to rapidly treat severe anaemia or blood loss, and used in sickle cell disease to prevent or manage complications. A life-saving measure in acute crises.

newTreatments.name: Early Developmental Intervention (FASD)
newTreatments.summary: Coordinated early therapies, structured routines, and educational and family support for children with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. Early, consistent intervention improves learning, behaviour, and long-term outcomes.

newTreatments.name: ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan, Heart Failure)
newTreatments.summary: A modern heart-failure medication combining two actions to relax blood vessels and reduce strain on the heart. As part of guideline-directed therapy it improves survival and reduces hospital admissions.

newTreatments.name: Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (e.g. Spironolactone)
newTreatments.summary: Medications that block a hormone driving fluid retention and heart strain, improving survival in heart failure and helping control resistant high blood pressure. A key pillar of guideline-directed heart-failure therapy.

newTreatments.name: Pain Management Program
newTreatments.summary: A structured, multidisciplinary approach combining medication, physical therapy, and coping strategies to manage chronic and crisis pain, such as in sickle cell disease and severe arthritis. Aims to restore function and quality of life.

newTreatments.name: ART Adherence Counselling and Support
newTreatments.summary: Structured counselling, education, and reminder support that helps people take their antiretroviral therapy consistently every day. Good adherence is what keeps the virus suppressed, protects the immune system, and makes HIV untransmittable, so this support is essential to treatment success rather than optional.

newTreatments.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
newTreatments.summary: Taken alongside isoniazid during TB treatment to prevent the nerve tingling and numbness (peripheral neuropathy) that isoniazid can cause. Routinely co-prescribed, especially for people with HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, or in pregnancy.

newTreatments.name: Nutritional Support
newTreatments.summary: Adequate protein and calorie intake, plus correcting deficiencies, to help the body recover from the weight loss and wasting that TB causes. An adjunct that supports recovery and improves treatment outcomes, never a replacement for TB antibiotics.

newTreatments.name: Montelukast (Leukotriene Receptor Antagonist)
newTreatments.summary: A daily anti-inflammatory tablet used as an add-on or alternative controller, particularly helpful for allergy-related and exercise-induced asthma. It is an add-on, not a replacement for a steroid inhaler.

newTreatments.name: Biologic Therapy for Severe Asthma (e.g. Omalizumab, Mepolizumab)
newTreatments.summary: Injectable targeted antibodies for severe, hard-to-control asthma that reduce flare-ups by blocking specific inflammatory pathways such as IgE or eosinophils. Reserved for severe disease that remains uncontrolled on inhalers.

newTreatments.name: Written Asthma Action Plan
newTreatments.summary: A personalised, clinician-written plan that guides daily inhaler use and how to step up treatment early during a flare, helping reduce emergency visits and hospital admissions.

newTreatments.name: Epilepsy Surgery
newTreatments.summary: Surgical removal or disconnection of the seizure-generating brain area, considered for drug-resistant focal epilepsy and potentially curative when a single seizure focus is identified.

newTreatments.name: Ketogenic Diet
newTreatments.summary: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate medically supervised diet used as an adjunct for drug-resistant epilepsy, especially in children, to reduce seizure frequency. It does not replace antiseizure medication.

newTreatments.name: Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS)
newTreatments.summary: An implanted device that sends regular mild electrical pulses to the vagus nerve, used as an add-on therapy to reduce seizure frequency in drug-resistant epilepsy.

newTreatments.name: Hydration (oral and IV fluids)
newTreatments.summary: Keeping well hydrated with fluids, and IV fluids during a crisis, helps prevent and ease vaso-occlusive pain episodes in sickle cell disease. A simple, central part of everyday self-care and acute management, used alongside (not instead of) hydroxyurea and infection prevention.

newTreatments.name: L-glutamine (Endari)
newTreatments.summary: An oral amino acid therapy shown to modestly reduce the frequency of pain crises in sickle cell disease. Used as an add-on to hydroxyurea where available, not as a replacement for it.

newTreatments.name: Pneumococcal vaccination (plus meningococcal, Hib, influenza)
newTreatments.summary: People with sickle cell disease have a damaged or absent spleen and are at high risk of life-threatening infection from pneumococcus and other bacteria. Pneumococcal vaccines (PCV and PPSV23), along with Hib, meningococcal and yearly flu vaccines, are a core preventive measure given alongside daily penicillin in young children.

newTreatments.name: Mechanical Thrombectomy (Endovascular Clot Removal)
newTreatments.summary: An emergency procedure for ischaemic (clot) stroke in which a catheter is threaded into the blocked brain artery and the clot is physically removed, restoring blood flow. For eligible large-vessel-occlusion strokes it is one of the most effective acute treatments for reducing long-term disability, generally within about 6 hours (sometimes up to 24 hours in selected patients).

newTreatments.name: Flu and Pneumococcal Vaccination
newTreatments.summary: Yearly influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination are recommended for people with COPD to lower the risk of chest infections that trigger dangerous flare-ups and hospital admissions.

newTreatments.name: Long-Term Oxygen Therapy
newTreatments.summary: For people with severe COPD and persistently low blood oxygen, breathing extra oxygen for at least 15 hours a day eases breathlessness and is one of the few treatments shown to help people live longer. Oxygen levels must be confirmed by testing first.

newTreatments.name: Intravenous Artesunate (Severe Malaria)
newTreatments.summary: The WHO first-line, life-saving treatment for severe or complicated malaria, given by injection in hospital. Large trials showed it lowers death rates compared with older quinine treatment, especially in African children.

newTreatments.name: Insecticide-Treated Bed Nets
newTreatments.summary: Long-lasting insecticidal nets that protect people from mosquito bites while they sleep. A cornerstone of malaria prevention that has substantially reduced infections and deaths across endemic regions.

newTreatments.name: Malaria Vaccine (RTS,S / R21)
newTreatments.summary: WHO-recommended vaccines that give children partial protection against malaria and reduce severe disease and deaths. Used alongside nets and prompt treatment rather than as a replacement for them.

newTreatments.name: Pegylated Interferon Alfa
newTreatments.summary: A weekly injection given for a fixed course (usually 48 weeks) that boosts the immune system to control hepatitis B. It can lead to a finite, off-treatment response in carefully selected patients but has more side effects than oral antivirals and is not suitable for advanced liver disease.

newTreatments.name: Hepatitis B Birth-Dose Vaccine
newTreatments.summary: A hepatitis B vaccine dose given within 24 hours of birth, which is the single most effective step to prevent mother-to-child transmission. It is a WHO-recommended cornerstone of eliminating hepatitis B in high-prevalence regions like Africa.

newTreatments.name: Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG)
newTreatments.summary: Ready-made antibodies given for rapid, short-term protection after exposure to hepatitis B, such as a newborn of an infected mother or after a needlestick injury. It is given alongside the vaccine to provide immediate cover while the vaccine builds lasting immunity.

newTreatments.name: Liver Transplant
newTreatments.summary: Replacement of a failing liver in people who develop end-stage liver disease or liver cancer from chronic hepatitis B. With antiviral medication and immunoglobulin to prevent reinfection of the new liver, long-term outcomes are very good.

newTreatments.name: Praziquantel repeat dose (4-6 weeks later)
newTreatments.summary: A second course of praziquantel given a few weeks after the first, because the drug does not kill immature worms; repeating the dose catches parasites that have since matured and raises cure rates.

newTreatments.name: Praziquantel mass drug administration (preventive chemotherapy)
newTreatments.summary: WHO-recommended community-wide deworming with praziquantel, especially for school-age children in endemic areas, to reduce worm burden, prevent complications, and lower transmission across the population.

newTreatments.name: Oxamniquine
newTreatments.summary: An older oral antiparasitic effective only against Schistosoma mansoni (intestinal bilharzia). Now rarely used and of limited availability since praziquantel covers all species, but a historical/backup option where praziquantel resistance or intolerance is a concern.

newTreatments.name: Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate) as adjunct
newTreatments.summary: Antimalarial drugs that also kill young, immature schistosome worms which praziquantel misses. Used in some settings alongside praziquantel or for prevention, complementing rather than replacing the standard cure.

newTreatments.name: Safe water access and improved sanitation
newTreatments.summary: Avoiding contact with potentially infested fresh water and using safe water plus proper toilets/latrines to prevent egg-contaminated urine and stool from reaching snail habitats. A key prevention and transmission-control measure, not a cure for existing infection.

newTreatments.name: Snail control (molluscicides and habitat management)
newTreatments.summary: Reducing the freshwater snails that host the parasite, through molluscicides or environmental management, to interrupt the transmission cycle at the community level. A public-health prevention measure that complements drug treatment, not an individual cure.

newTreatments.name: Leflunomide (DMARD)
newTreatments.summary: A conventional synthetic DMARD that suppresses overactive immune cells, used alone or alongside methotrexate to control rheumatoid arthritis when methotrexate isn't suitable or isn't enough.

newTreatments.name: Intra-articular Corticosteroid Injection
newTreatments.summary: A steroid injected directly into the affected joint to reduce inflammation and provide short-term pain relief during flares; benefit typically lasts weeks to a few months and injections are limited per year.

newTreatments.name: Belimumab (Biologic for Lupus)
newTreatments.summary: A targeted biologic (B-lymphocyte stimulator inhibitor) approved for systemic lupus, used as add-on therapy to reduce flares and steroid dependence in active disease, including lupus nephritis.

newTreatments.name: Sun Protection (UV Avoidance & Sunscreen)
newTreatments.summary: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, and avoiding peak UV are important in lupus because sunlight commonly triggers skin and systemic flares. A core preventive measure alongside medication, not a replacement for it.

newTreatments.name: Febuxostat (Urate-Lowering Therapy)
newTreatments.summary: A xanthine-oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid, used as an alternative urate-lowering therapy when allopurinol is not tolerated or fails to reach the target urate level.

newTreatments.name: Low-Purine Diet
newTreatments.summary: Reducing high-purine foods such as red and organ meats, shellfish, and sugary drinks to help lower uric acid as an adjunct to medication, not a replacement for it.

newTreatments.name: Alcohol Reduction
newTreatments.summary: Cutting back on alcohol, especially beer and spirits, to reduce uric-acid spikes and lower the frequency of gout flares alongside medical treatment.

newTreatments.name: Vitamin C Supplement
newTreatments.summary: Vitamin C may modestly lower serum uric acid; an emerging-evidence adjunct only, not a substitute for urate-lowering medication.

newTreatments.name: Deworming Therapy (e.g. Albendazole/Mebendazole)
newTreatments.summary: Antiparasitic tablets that clear intestinal worms such as hookworm, a major and treatable cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in Africa. Used alongside iron replacement to stop ongoing blood and iron loss when worms are the cause.

newTreatments.name: Vitamin C (with iron)
newTreatments.summary: Taking vitamin C, or eating vitamin-C-rich foods, with iron tablets boosts how much iron the gut absorbs. An inexpensive adjunct that makes iron repletion more effective, not a stand-alone treatment.

newTreatments.name: Iron-Rich Diet
newTreatments.summary: Eating more iron-rich foods like red meat, liver, beans, lentils, and dark leafy greens helps maintain iron levels and prevent relapse. A supportive measure that complements, but cannot replace, medical iron treatment in established anaemia.

newTreatments.name: Clozapine
newTreatments.summary: The most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, used when two other antipsychotics have not worked. It requires regular blood monitoring because of a rare risk to white blood cells, but can be life-changing for symptoms that have not responded to other medicines.

newTreatments.name: Motivational Interviewing / Enhancement Therapy
newTreatments.summary: A collaborative, non-judgemental counselling style that strengthens a person's own motivation to change drinking. Strong evidence in alcohol use disorder, especially as a brief intervention and to engage people in further treatment.

newTreatments.name: Structured Exercise Program
newTreatments.summary: Regular aerobic and strength activity used as an adjunct in recovery to reduce cravings, improve mood and sleep, and support overall health. Helpful alongside — never instead of — counselling and relapse-prevention medication.

newTreatments.name: Surgery (Radical Hysterectomy / Conization)
newTreatments.summary: Surgical removal of the cancer, ranging from a cone biopsy or trachelectomy for very early disease to a radical hysterectomy removing the cervix, uterus, and nearby tissue. Often curative for early-stage cervical cancer.

newTreatments.name: Concurrent Chemoradiation (with Brachytherapy)
newTreatments.summary: The standard curative treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer: cisplatin-based chemotherapy given alongside external-beam radiation plus internal radiation (brachytherapy) to maximise tumour control.

conditions.name: HIV
conditions.summary: HIV is a virus that gradually weakens the immune system, but it is now a manageable lifelong condition, not a death sentence. With daily antiretroviral therapy taken consistently, people live long, healthy lives and the virus becomes undetectable and untransmittable to others (U=U).

symptoms.name: Frequent or persistent infections (e.g. thrush, shingles, TB)

triggers.name: Condomless sex with a partner whose status or viral load is unknown
Missed antiretroviral doses (poor adherence, leading to viral rebound)
Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding

tests.name: HIV antibody/antigen rapid or blood test
HIV RNA PCR (early detection / infant diagnosis)

extraTreatments.name: ART Adherence Counselling and Support
extraTreatments.summary: Structured counselling, education, and reminder support that helps people take their antiretroviral therapy consistently every day. Good adherence is what keeps the virus suppressed, protects the immune system, and makes HIV untransmittable, so this support is essential to treatment success rather than optional.

conditions.name: Tuberculosis
conditions.summary: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection, usually of the lungs, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spread through the air when someone coughs. The good news is that it is curable: a full course of TB antibiotics taken every day for the whole treatment period clears the infection, and finishing every dose is what stops the disease from coming back or becoming drug-resistant.

symptoms.name: Chest pain when breathing or coughing

triggers.name: Close-contact exposure to an active TB case
Crowded or poorly ventilated living conditions

extraTreatments.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
extraTreatments.summary: Taken alongside isoniazid during TB treatment to prevent the nerve tingling and numbness (peripheral neuropathy) that isoniazid can cause. Routinely co-prescribed, especially for people with HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, or in pregnancy.

extraTreatments.name: Nutritional Support
extraTreatments.summary: Adequate protein and calorie intake, plus correcting deficiencies, to help the body recover from the weight loss and wasting that TB causes. An adjunct that supports recovery and improves treatment outcomes, never a replacement for TB antibiotics.

conditions.name: Hypertension
conditions.summary: Hypertension means your blood pressure stays higher than healthy over time, which quietly strains your heart, brain, and kidneys long before you feel anything. The good news is that it is very manageable: daily blood-pressure medication together with small lifestyle changes like cutting salt, moving more, and losing a little weight keeps it well controlled and dramatically lowers your risk of stroke and heart disease.

conditions.name: Asthma
conditions.summary: Asthma is a common long-term condition where the airways become inflamed and tighten, causing wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and breathlessness that come and go. With a daily preventer (steroid) inhaler and a reliever inhaler on hand, most people control their symptoms well and live full, active lives.

extraTreatments.name: Montelukast (Leukotriene Receptor Antagonist)
extraTreatments.summary: A daily anti-inflammatory tablet used as an add-on or alternative controller, particularly helpful for allergy-related and exercise-induced asthma. It is an add-on, not a replacement for a steroid inhaler.

extraTreatments.name: Biologic Therapy for Severe Asthma (e.g. Omalizumab, Mepolizumab)
extraTreatments.summary: Injectable targeted antibodies for severe, hard-to-control asthma that reduce flare-ups by blocking specific inflammatory pathways such as IgE or eosinophils. Reserved for severe disease that remains uncontrolled on inhalers.

extraTreatments.name: Written Asthma Action Plan
extraTreatments.summary: A personalised, clinician-written plan that guides daily inhaler use and how to step up treatment early during a flare, helping reduce emergency visits and hospital admissions.

conditions.name: Epilepsy
conditions.summary: Epilepsy is a condition where the brain produces recurring seizures, and although it carries a heavy burden in Africa with many people still untreated, it is very manageable. With the right daily antiseizure medication, most people gain good seizure control and live full, active lives.

symptoms.name: Confusion and drowsiness after a seizure (postictal state)
Loss of awareness or staring spells
Uncontrolled jerking or convulsions of arms and legs
Aura or warning sensation before a seizure
Memory, mood, or concentration difficulties between seizures
Tongue biting or loss of bladder control during seizures

triggers.name: Missed or skipped antiseizure medication doses

tests.name: Detailed seizure history and clinical examination

extraTreatments.name: Epilepsy Surgery
extraTreatments.summary: Surgical removal or disconnection of the seizure-generating brain area, considered for drug-resistant focal epilepsy and potentially curative when a single seizure focus is identified.

extraTreatments.name: Ketogenic Diet
extraTreatments.summary: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate medically supervised diet used as an adjunct for drug-resistant epilepsy, especially in children, to reduce seizure frequency. It does not replace antiseizure medication.

extraTreatments.name: Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS)
extraTreatments.summary: An implanted device that sends regular mild electrical pulses to the vagus nerve, used as an add-on therapy to reduce seizure frequency in drug-resistant epilepsy.

conditions.name: Sickle Cell Disease
conditions.summary: Sickle Cell Disease is an inherited blood condition where red blood cells take on a rigid, sickle shape, blocking blood flow and causing episodes of severe pain, anaemia, and a higher risk of infection. With the right care, hydroxyurea, vaccines and daily antibiotics to prevent infection, staying well hydrated, and good pain management, most people can live full lives and have fewer crises.

triggers.name: Cold weather or sudden temperature change

tests.name: Full blood count with reticulocytes and blood film

extraTreatments.name: Hydration (oral and IV fluids)
extraTreatments.summary: Keeping well hydrated with fluids, and IV fluids during a crisis, helps prevent and ease vaso-occlusive pain episodes in sickle cell disease. A simple, central part of everyday self-care and acute management, used alongside (not instead of) hydroxyurea and infection prevention.

extraTreatments.name: L-glutamine (Endari)
extraTreatments.summary: An oral amino acid therapy shown to modestly reduce the frequency of pain crises in sickle cell disease. Used as an add-on to hydroxyurea where available, not as a replacement for it.

extraTreatments.name: Pneumococcal vaccination (plus meningococcal, Hib, influenza)
extraTreatments.summary: People with sickle cell disease have a damaged or absent spleen and are at high risk of life-threatening infection from pneumococcus and other bacteria. Pneumococcal vaccines (PCV and PPSV23), along with Hib, meningococcal and yearly flu vaccines, are a core preventive measure given alongside daily penicillin in young children.

conditions.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
conditions.summary: Chronic kidney disease means your kidneys are slowly losing their ability to filter waste and extra fluid from your blood, most often because of long-standing high blood pressure, diabetes, or HIV. The encouraging news is that controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, treating HIV, and newer kidney-protecting medicines can slow it down a lot, and even when the kidneys fail, dialysis or a transplant can keep you living well.

symptoms.name: Swelling in legs, ankles, or face (oedema)
Frothy or foamy urine (protein in urine)
Poor appetite, nausea, or a metallic taste

triggers.name: NSAID painkillers and nephrotoxic medicines or herbal remedies

tests.name: Blood test for creatinine and estimated GFR (eGFR)
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR / dipstick for protein)

conditions.name: Stroke
conditions.summary: A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is suddenly interrupted, either by a clot blocking a vessel (ischaemic) or by a bleed (haemorrhagic), so brain cells begin to die within minutes. Getting to hospital fast is critical, and for clot strokes clot-busting or clot-removal treatment can save brain tissue; with rehabilitation and steady control of blood pressure, many people recover function and lower their risk of another stroke.

symptoms.name: Sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body (arm, leg, or face)
Slurred speech or difficulty speaking or understanding words
Loss of balance, dizziness, or trouble walking
Sudden vision loss or double vision in one or both eyes
Sudden severe headache with no known cause

triggers.name: Previous stroke or transient ischaemic attack (mini-stroke)

tests.name: CT scan of the brain (to distinguish clot from bleed)
Blood pressure, blood glucose, and cholesterol testing

extraTreatments.name: Mechanical Thrombectomy (Endovascular Clot Removal)
extraTreatments.summary: An emergency procedure for ischaemic (clot) stroke in which a catheter is threaded into the blocked brain artery and the clot is physically removed, restoring blood flow. For eligible large-vessel-occlusion strokes it is one of the most effective acute treatments for reducing long-term disability, generally within about 6 hours (sometimes up to 24 hours in selected patients).

conditions.name: COPD
conditions.summary: COPD is a long-term lung condition where the airways narrow and become inflamed, making it harder to breathe out fully — most often from smoking, but also from cooking-fire smoke and other indoor air pollution common across Africa. It can't be reversed, but stopping smoking, inhalers, pulmonary rehab, and vaccinations can ease breathlessness, cut down flare-ups, and help you stay active and well for years.

extraTreatments.name: Flu and Pneumococcal Vaccination
extraTreatments.summary: Yearly influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination are recommended for people with COPD to lower the risk of chest infections that trigger dangerous flare-ups and hospital admissions.

extraTreatments.name: Long-Term Oxygen Therapy
extraTreatments.summary: For people with severe COPD and persistently low blood oxygen, breathing extra oxygen for at least 15 hours a day eases breathlessness and is one of the few treatments shown to help people live longer. Oxygen levels must be confirmed by testing first.

conditions.name: Malaria
conditions.summary: Malaria is an infection caused by Plasmodium parasites spread through the bite of an infected mosquito, and it is very common across much of sub-Saharan Africa. The good news is that it is curable: when treatment is started quickly with the right antimalarial medicines (artemisinin-based combination therapy), most people recover fully, and simple steps like sleeping under a treated net help keep you safe.

triggers.name: Travel to a high-transmission region without prophylaxis

tests.name: Full blood count (checks anaemia and platelets)

extraTreatments.name: Intravenous Artesunate (Severe Malaria)
extraTreatments.summary: The WHO first-line, life-saving treatment for severe or complicated malaria, given by injection in hospital. Large trials showed it lowers death rates compared with older quinine treatment, especially in African children.

extraTreatments.name: Insecticide-Treated Bed Nets
extraTreatments.summary: Long-lasting insecticidal nets that protect people from mosquito bites while they sleep. A cornerstone of malaria prevention that has substantially reduced infections and deaths across endemic regions.

extraTreatments.name: Malaria Vaccine (RTS,S / R21)
extraTreatments.summary: WHO-recommended vaccines that give children partial protection against malaria and reduce severe disease and deaths. Used alongside nets and prompt treatment rather than as a replacement for them.

conditions.name: Hepatitis B
conditions.summary: Hepatitis B is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus, which is common across Africa and is often carried for years without any symptoms. The good news is that a safe vaccine can prevent it, and daily antiviral tablets can keep the virus under control and protect your liver, even though they don't fully cure it.

symptoms.name: Pain or discomfort over the liver (right upper abdomen)

triggers.name: Unprotected sex or contact with infected blood
Sharing needles, razors, or unsterile medical/tattoo equipment
Heavy alcohol use accelerating liver damage
Co-infection with HIV or hepatitis C

tests.name: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) blood test
Liver ultrasound / FibroScan and HBeAg testing

extraTreatments.name: Pegylated Interferon Alfa
extraTreatments.summary: A weekly injection given for a fixed course (usually 48 weeks) that boosts the immune system to control hepatitis B. It can lead to a finite, off-treatment response in carefully selected patients but has more side effects than oral antivirals and is not suitable for advanced liver disease.

extraTreatments.name: Hepatitis B Birth-Dose Vaccine
extraTreatments.summary: A hepatitis B vaccine dose given within 24 hours of birth, which is the single most effective step to prevent mother-to-child transmission. It is a WHO-recommended cornerstone of eliminating hepatitis B in high-prevalence regions like Africa.

extraTreatments.name: Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG)
extraTreatments.summary: Ready-made antibodies given for rapid, short-term protection after exposure to hepatitis B, such as a newborn of an infected mother or after a needlestick injury. It is given alongside the vaccine to provide immediate cover while the vaccine builds lasting immunity.

extraTreatments.name: Liver Transplant
extraTreatments.summary: Replacement of a failing liver in people who develop end-stage liver disease or liver cancer from chronic hepatitis B. With antiviral medication and immunoglobulin to prevent reinfection of the new liver, long-term outcomes are very good.

conditions.name: Schistosomiasis
conditions.summary: Schistosomiasis (also called bilharzia or snail fever) is a parasitic infection caught from freshwater where certain snails live, common in parts of South Africa and across Africa. The good news is that a single course of the tablet praziquantel cures most people, and getting treated early prevents long-term damage to the bladder, bowel, and liver.

symptoms.name: Itchy rash at site of water contact (swimmer's itch)
Fever, chills and muscle aches (acute Katayama)
Genital sores or discharge (female/male genital schistosomiasis)

triggers.name: Swimming, wading or bathing in infested fresh water (lakes, rivers, dams)
Living in or travelling to an endemic rural area
Occupational water contact (farming, fishing, washing clothes)
Poor sanitation and contaminated water sources near snail habitats
Childhood exposure and repeated re-infection without treatment

tests.name: Urine microscopy for parasite eggs (S. haematobium)
Stool microscopy for parasite eggs (S. mansoni / Kato-Katz)
Antibody/antigen serology or ultrasound for organ involvement

extraTreatments.name: Praziquantel repeat dose (4-6 weeks later)
extraTreatments.summary: A second course of praziquantel given a few weeks after the first, because the drug does not kill immature worms; repeating the dose catches parasites that have since matured and raises cure rates.

extraTreatments.name: Praziquantel mass drug administration (preventive chemotherapy)
extraTreatments.summary: WHO-recommended community-wide deworming with praziquantel, especially for school-age children in endemic areas, to reduce worm burden, prevent complications, and lower transmission across the population.

extraTreatments.name: Oxamniquine
extraTreatments.summary: An older oral antiparasitic effective only against Schistosoma mansoni (intestinal bilharzia). Now rarely used and of limited availability since praziquantel covers all species, but a historical/backup option where praziquantel resistance or intolerance is a concern.

extraTreatments.name: Artemisinin derivatives (artesunate) as adjunct
extraTreatments.summary: Antimalarial drugs that also kill young, immature schistosome worms which praziquantel misses. Used in some settings alongside praziquantel or for prevention, complementing rather than replacing the standard cure.

extraTreatments.name: Safe water access and improved sanitation
extraTreatments.summary: Avoiding contact with potentially infested fresh water and using safe water plus proper toilets/latrines to prevent egg-contaminated urine and stool from reaching snail habitats. A key prevention and transmission-control measure, not a cure for existing infection.

extraTreatments.name: Snail control (molluscicides and habitat management)
extraTreatments.summary: Reducing the freshwater snails that host the parasite, through molluscicides or environmental management, to interrupt the transmission cycle at the community level. A public-health prevention measure that complements drug treatment, not an individual cure.

conditions.name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
conditions.summary: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where your immune system attacks the lining of your joints, causing pain, swelling, and stiffness that's often worst in the morning. Starting DMARD medication like methotrexate early can calm the inflammation, protect your joints from lasting damage, and help many people reach low disease activity or remission.

extraTreatments.name: Leflunomide (DMARD)
extraTreatments.summary: A conventional synthetic DMARD that suppresses overactive immune cells, used alone or alongside methotrexate to control rheumatoid arthritis when methotrexate isn't suitable or isn't enough.

conditions.name: Osteoarthritis
conditions.summary: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, where the smooth cartilage that cushions a joint gradually wears down, leading to pain, stiffness, and reduced movement, most often in the knees, hips, hands, and spine. The good news is that staying active, keeping to a healthy weight, and good pain control help most people stay mobile, and for badly worn joints, replacement surgery can dramatically restore comfort and function.

symptoms.name: Joint pain that worsens with activity and eases with rest
Joint stiffness, especially in the morning or after resting (typically under 30 minutes)
Reduced range of motion and difficulty moving the joint
Grating or crackling sensation (crepitus) when the joint moves
Bony swelling or enlargement around the joint (e.g. finger nodes)
Muscle weakness around the affected joint
Joint instability or a feeling the joint may give way

triggers.name: Excess body weight (extra load on knees and hips)
Previous joint injury or repetitive overuse
Overexertion or sudden increase in physical activity

tests.name: Clinical examination and history (the primary basis for diagnosis)
X-ray of the affected joint (shows joint-space narrowing, osteophytes)
Blood tests to rule out inflammatory arthritis (e.g. RA, gout)
MRI scan (when diagnosis is unclear or for detailed assessment)

extraTreatments.name: Intra-articular Corticosteroid Injection
extraTreatments.summary: A steroid injected directly into the affected joint to reduce inflammation and provide short-term pain relief during flares; benefit typically lasts weeks to a few months and injections are limited per year.

conditions.name: Lupus (SLE)
conditions.summary: Lupus is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues, causing inflammation that can affect the skin, joints, kidneys, blood, and other organs, often with flares and quieter periods. It tends to be more common and more severe in people of African ancestry, but with the right long-term medication, most people can control their symptoms and protect their organs.

tests.name: Complement levels (C3, C4) and full blood count
Urine test and kidney biopsy (for nephritis)

extraTreatments.name: Belimumab (Biologic for Lupus)
extraTreatments.summary: A targeted biologic (B-lymphocyte stimulator inhibitor) approved for systemic lupus, used as add-on therapy to reduce flares and steroid dependence in active disease, including lupus nephritis.

extraTreatments.name: Sun Protection (UV Avoidance & Sunscreen)
extraTreatments.summary: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, protective clothing, and avoiding peak UV are important in lupus because sunlight commonly triggers skin and systemic flares. A core preventive measure alongside medication, not a replacement for it.

conditions.name: Gout
conditions.summary: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by sharp uric-acid crystals building up in a joint, often triggering sudden, intensely painful attacks that frequently start in the big toe. The good news is that it is very treatable: daily urate-lowering medication like allopurinol can prevent future attacks for most people, while anti-inflammatories settle a flare when one strikes.

symptoms.name: Sudden, severe joint pain (often the big toe)
Warmth and tenderness in the joint
Limited range of motion in the joint
Peeling, itchy skin as the flare settles
Tophi (hard urate lumps under the skin)

triggers.name: Purine-rich foods (red meat, organ meat, shellfish)
Diuretics or sudden changes in urate-lowering medication

tests.name: Joint fluid analysis for urate crystals
Kidney function and metabolic blood panel
Ultrasound or dual-energy CT of the joint

extraTreatments.name: Febuxostat (Urate-Lowering Therapy)
extraTreatments.summary: A xanthine-oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid, used as an alternative urate-lowering therapy when allopurinol is not tolerated or fails to reach the target urate level.

extraTreatments.name: Low-Purine Diet
extraTreatments.summary: Reducing high-purine foods such as red and organ meats, shellfish, and sugary drinks to help lower uric acid as an adjunct to medication, not a replacement for it.

extraTreatments.name: Alcohol Reduction
extraTreatments.summary: Cutting back on alcohol, especially beer and spirits, to reduce uric-acid spikes and lower the frequency of gout flares alongside medical treatment.

extraTreatments.name: Vitamin C Supplement
extraTreatments.summary: Vitamin C may modestly lower serum uric acid; an emerging-evidence adjunct only, not a substitute for urate-lowering medication.

conditions.name: Iron-Deficiency Anaemia
conditions.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia happens when your body doesn't have enough iron to make healthy red blood cells, which can leave you tired, pale, and short of breath. The good news is that it's very treatable: replacing the iron and finding and fixing the cause of the loss almost always brings your blood count and energy back to normal.

symptoms.name: Pallor (pale skin, lips, and inner eyelids)

triggers.name: Poor dietary iron intake or low-iron diet

tests.name: Iron studies (serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation)
Stool test for parasites or occult blood

extraTreatments.name: Deworming Therapy (e.g. Albendazole/Mebendazole)
extraTreatments.summary: Antiparasitic tablets that clear intestinal worms such as hookworm, a major and treatable cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in Africa. Used alongside iron replacement to stop ongoing blood and iron loss when worms are the cause.

extraTreatments.name: Vitamin C (with iron)
extraTreatments.summary: Taking vitamin C, or eating vitamin-C-rich foods, with iron tablets boosts how much iron the gut absorbs. An inexpensive adjunct that makes iron repletion more effective, not a stand-alone treatment.

extraTreatments.name: Iron-Rich Diet
extraTreatments.summary: Eating more iron-rich foods like red meat, liver, beans, lentils, and dark leafy greens helps maintain iron levels and prevent relapse. A supportive measure that complements, but cannot replace, medical iron treatment in established anaemia.

conditions.name: Schizophrenia
conditions.summary: Schizophrenia is a serious but treatable mental illness that can affect how a person thinks, feels, and tells apart what is real, often bringing hallucinations, strong beliefs others do not share, and changes in motivation or emotion. With steady antipsychotic medication and good support from family and a care team, many people manage their symptoms well and live full, meaningful lives.

symptoms.name: Lack of insight into being unwell

tests.name: Bloods and brain imaging to exclude other causes

extraTreatments.name: Clozapine
extraTreatments.summary: The most effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, used when two other antipsychotics have not worked. It requires regular blood monitoring because of a rare risk to white blood cells, but can be life-changing for symptoms that have not responded to other medicines.

conditions.name: Alcohol Use Disorder
conditions.summary: Alcohol Use Disorder is a treatable condition where drinking becomes hard to control and starts to harm your health, relationships, or daily life, despite wanting to cut down. Recovery is very possible: a combination of counselling, peer support, and relapse-prevention medication helps many people drink less or stop, and reaching out for help is a sign of strength rather than weakness.

symptoms.name: Craving — a strong urge or compulsion to drink
Loss of control over how much or how often you drink
Continuing to drink despite harm to health, work, or relationships
Tolerance — needing more alcohol for the same effect
Failed attempts to cut down or stop
Neglecting responsibilities or activities you used to enjoy
Spending a lot of time drinking or recovering from drinking
Withdrawal symptoms (shaking, sweating, anxiety, nausea) when not drinking

triggers.name: Social settings, peer pressure, and easy alcohol availability
Cues and routines linked to drinking (places, people, times of day)

tests.name: Liver function tests and GGT (blood test)
Full blood count including MCV (red-cell size)

extraTreatments.name: Motivational Interviewing / Enhancement Therapy
extraTreatments.summary: A collaborative, non-judgemental counselling style that strengthens a person's own motivation to change drinking. Strong evidence in alcohol use disorder, especially as a brief intervention and to engage people in further treatment.

extraTreatments.name: Structured Exercise Program
extraTreatments.summary: Regular aerobic and strength activity used as an adjunct in recovery to reduce cravings, improve mood and sleep, and support overall health. Helpful alongside — never instead of — counselling and relapse-prevention medication.

conditions.name: Cervical Cancer
conditions.summary: Cervical cancer develops in the cells of the cervix and is almost always caused by long-term infection with high-risk HPV, with HIV greatly raising the risk. The encouraging news is that it is one of the most preventable and, when caught early, most treatable cancers: HPV vaccination and regular screening stop most cases, while surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy can cure or control disease that has already developed.

symptoms.name: Abnormal vaginal bleeding (between periods, after sex, or after menopause)
Pain or bleeding during or after sex
Heavier or prolonged irregular vaginal bleeding

triggers.name: Early or multiple sexual partners without protection

tests.name: Cervical screening (Pap smear / HPV test / VIA)
Pelvic exam and staging imaging (MRI / CT / ultrasound)

extraTreatments.name: Surgery (Radical Hysterectomy / Conization)
extraTreatments.summary: Surgical removal of the cancer, ranging from a cone biopsy or trachelectomy for very early disease to a radical hysterectomy removing the cervix, uterus, and nearby tissue. Often curative for early-stage cervical cancer.

extraTreatments.name: Concurrent Chemoradiation (with Brachytherapy)
extraTreatments.summary: The standard curative treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer: cisplatin-based chemotherapy given alongside external-beam radiation plus internal radiation (brachytherapy) to maximise tumour control.

conditions.name: Heart Failure
conditions.summary: Heart failure means the heart can't pump strongly enough to meet the body's needs, often after years of high blood pressure, a damaged heart valve, or a previous heart attack. It is a serious but very treatable condition: the right combination of daily medicines, salt and fluid awareness, and regular check-ups can ease breathlessness and swelling, keep you out of hospital, and help you live longer.

symptoms.name: Swelling of the legs, ankles, or feet (oedema)
Waking at night gasping for breath (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)
Sudden weight gain from fluid build-up

conditions.name: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
conditions.summary: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder is a lifelong condition caused by alcohol exposure before birth, which affects how the brain and body develop and can lead to differences in learning, behaviour, and sometimes physical features. There is no cure, but starting support early and building a structured, predictable, and understanding environment at home and school makes a real difference to how well a person thrives.

symptoms.name: Learning difficulties and low IQ / intellectual disability
Poor impulse control and difficulty understanding consequences
Delayed speech, language, and motor development
Emotional dysregulation, anxiety, and behavioural problems
Distinctive facial features (small eye openings, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip)
Slow growth and small head size (microcephaly)

triggers.name: Any alcohol use during pregnancy (the underlying cause of the condition)
Heavy or binge drinking in pregnancy (higher risk and severity)
Unstructured, unpredictable, or chaotic environments worsening behaviour
Overstimulation, sensory overload, and changes in routine
Late diagnosis and lack of early support

tests.name: Clinical assessment of facial features and growth (dysmorphology exam)
History of confirmed (or, where records are missing, presumed) prenatal alcohol exposure
Neurodevelopmental and cognitive (IQ / behavioural / executive function) assessment
